steps.label: Do Now: Find the Wrong Statements (1 of 2)
steps.content:
Do Now: Find the Wrong Statements (1 of 2)

Cambridge IGCSE 0478/12 March 2024 Q2(a). What to do: type your answer, then press Check my answer or Submit answer.

A computer has a central processing unit (CPU). The table contains five statements about the role of registers in a CPU. Two of the statements are not correct.

LetterStatement
APC stores the address of the next instruction to be accessed
BMAR stores the instructions of the program that is running
CMDR stores the data passed to it from the PC
DACC stores the result of each calculation
ECIR stores the instruction currently being executed

items.prompt: Identify the letter of each incorrect statement. Suggest a corrected statement for each.
scheme: ... the MAR stores addresses, not instructions
... the data comes from the (data) bus, not the PC // the data comes from the address in the MAR, not the PC
items.guidance: One mark for each incorrect letter (B and C) and one mark for its matching correction. A correction earns its mark only with its letter. A correct letter with a wrong correction earns 1 of 2.
items.modelAnswer: B: the MAR stores addresses, not instructions. C: the MDR gets data from the address in the MAR, not the PC.

walkthrough.title: Walk me through it: find the wrong statement

steps.text: A similar question. Two statements about the CPU. One is not correct. Find it, then correct it.
steps.visual:
P: The ALU carries out calculations.

Q: The CU carries out calculations.

steps.text: Read each statement and ask: is this the real job of that part? P: the ALU does carry out calculations. P is correct.
steps.visual: ALU carries out calculations: correct

steps.text: Q: the CU does not carry out calculations. The CU is in charge: it sends control signals. So Q is not correct.
Correct it: keep the part, and give its real job. "The CU sends control signals to the other parts." The letter is 1 mark, the correction is 1 mark.
Now do the same for A to E: for each register, what does it really hold, and where does it get it from? Two statements are wrong.

Do Now: The MAR (2 of 2)

Recap of the last two lessons. Cambridge IGCSE 0478/13, June 2022, Question 5(b)(ii). The memory address register (MAR) is one component built into the CPU. What to do: type your answer, then press Check my answer or Submit answer.

items.prompt: Describe the purpose of the MAR in the CPU.
scheme: ... the address of the next data or instructions required
... the address of the location in memory where data is to be stored
It stores the address that is to be collected by the address bus
items.guidance: Any two from the points, one mark each. Points 2 and 3 follow on from point 1. "It stores data" with no address earns no mark.
items.modelAnswer: It temporarily stores the address of the next data or instruction needed.

walkthrough.title: Walk me through it: describe a register's purpose

steps.text: A similar question. "Describe the purpose of the MDR in the CPU." It is worth 2 marks.
Point 1: what kind of thing does it hold? The MDR holds data or an instruction.
steps.visual: the MDR holds data or an instruction

steps.text: Point 2: which data, from where? The data that has just come from memory.
steps.visual: ... that has come from memory

steps.visual: what it holds + where from = 2 marks

steps.text: Now the MAR: what kind of thing does it hold, and which one? Where does it go next?
steps.visual: what kind? which one? where next?

steps.label: The Fetch-Decode-Execute Cycle
steps.content:
3.1 Computer Architecture

The Fetch-Decode-Execute Cycle

Year 10

  • Today: how the CPU runs a program, one small move at a time, and why each move happens.
  • One tiny memory all lesson: four addresses, two instructions, two numbers.
  • How this lesson works: on each slide, look at the picture, predict by picking an answer, then read why.
Think → Pair → ShareLast lesson, the CPU read a value from memory on the buses. Predict: what does the CPU need to read from memory to run a program?Show the answer

The instructions of the program, and the data they use. Both are stored in memory.

items.prompt: Predict: LOAD 6 is stored in memory at address 4. What must happen before the CPU can carry it out?
options: A copy of LOAD 6 must come into the CPU
Nothing: the CPU carries it out inside memory
Memory must carry out LOAD 6 itself
items.explain: A copy must come into the CPU, because the CPU can only work on what is inside it. Copying the next instruction from memory into the CPU is called fetch. It is the first stage.

steps.label: Compare: What If the PC Stayed at 4?

Compare: What If the PC Stayed at 4?

What to do: compare the two CPUs, then pick your prediction. The reason appears under it.

CPU A: the PC goes up by 1
After fetching LOAD 6, the PC holds 5.
The next fetch reads address 5: ADD 7.
CPU B: the PC stays the same
After fetching LOAD 6, the PC still holds 4.
The next fetch reads address 4: ?

items.prompt: Predict: what goes wrong in CPU B?
options: Nothing: memory knows what comes next
It fetches LOAD 6 again and again
items.explain: Every fetch in CPU B reads address 4, so it fetches LOAD 6 again and again and never moves on. That is why the PC goes up by 1 in every fetch.

items.prompt: Predict: why is LOAD 6 copied from the MDR into the CIR?

items.explain: Everything that comes from memory arrives in the MDR. When the number from address 6 arrives, it replaces what was there. So LOAD 6 is copied into the CIR first, on the data bus, and kept safe inside the CU. This is the last move of fetch.

items.prompt: Predict: why must the CU work out what the instruction means before anything else happens?
options: The ALU can only add numbers
Each instruction needs different parts to do different jobs
The instruction must be sent back to memory
items.explain: Each instruction is different, so the CU must know which parts to use before anything is done. Working out what an instruction means is called decode. The CU uses the instruction set (the list of commands the CPU can carry out) to decode it.

steps.label: Compare: LOAD 6 and ADD 6
steps.content:
Compare: LOAD 6 and ADD 6

What to do: compare the two instructions, then pick your prediction. The reason appears under it.

LOAD 6
It names address 6.
Address 6 holds 12.
ADD 6
It names address 6.
Address 6 holds 12.

items.prompt: Predict: both name address 6. What is different about them once they are decoded?
options: Nothing: they do the same job
What is done with the number from address 6
items.explain: Both read the 12 at address 6. LOAD copies it into the ACC. ADD makes the ALU add it to the ACC. Decoding tells the CU which of these to do.

items.prompt: Predict: what does the CPU do next?
items.explain: It goes back to fetch, using the address in the PC: 5. It fetches ADD 7, decodes it and executes it, then fetches the next one. The same three stages repeat for every instruction, so it is called the fetch-decode-execute (FDE) cycle.

What to do: pick the stage for each move. Ask: is the instruction coming in, being worked out, or being carried out? Done when both are answered.

items.prompt: The PC goes up by 1. Which stage is this?
items.explain: Fetch. The PC goes up by 1 while the instruction is being fetched, so it holds the address of the next one.

items.prompt: The ALU works out 12 + 30. Which stage is this?
items.explain: Execute. The instruction ADD 7 has been fetched and decoded; now it is carried out.

Cambridge IGCSE 0478/11, November 2024, Question 5(b). A central processing unit (CPU) performs the fetch-decode-execute (FDE) cycle. What to do: type your answer, then press Check my answer or Submit answer.

items.prompt: (b) Describe what happens at the decode stage of the cycle.
scheme: The CIR or CU receives the instruction from the MDR // the instruction is sent from the MDR to the CIR or CU
The instruction is separated into opcode and operand
The control unit decodes the instruction
items.guidance: Any three, one mark each. Point 2 follows on from point 1, and point 5 follows on from point 4. "The instruction is decoded" with no CU earns no mark for point 4.

Cambridge IGCSE 0478/11, June 2024, Question 5(d) (adapted: describe, not draw and annotate). The computer processes instructions using the fetch-decode-execute (FDE) cycle. What to do: type your answer, then press Check my answer or Submit answer.

items.prompt: Describe the process of the fetch stage of the FDE cycle.
scheme: Names the registers MAR, MDR and PC
The address is sent from the PC to the MAR
The address is sent from the MAR to RAM
The data or instruction is sent from RAM to the MDR
The data or instruction is sent from the MDR to the CIR or CU
The control unit sends a control signal for any part of the process
items.guidance: Any four, one mark each. The address bus, data bus and control bus marks can be given anywhere they are used correctly. A point marked ... follows on from the point before it.
items.modelAnswer: The PC sends the address to the MAR on the address bus, then the PC is incremented. The instruction is sent from RAM to the MDR.
